name: ICF syndrome (DNMT3B)
aliases: immunodeficiency centromeric instability and facial anomalies syndrome

reference.source: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders / IUIS classification of inborn errors of immunity
clinicalPearls: A rare syndrome uniting immunodeficiency, centromeric chromosomal instability and characteristic facial anomalies, hence the name ICF

The predominant immune defect is a humoral one, with variable hypogammaglobulinaemia or agammaglobulinaemia despite the frequent presence of B cells, causing recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infection
The cytogenetic hallmark is instability of the pericentromeric heterochromatin of chromosomes 1, 9 and 16, seen as multiradial figures and stretched or decondensed regions on karyotype
Facial features can include hypertelorism, a flat nasal bridge, epicanthic folds and low-set ears, alongside developmental delay in many patients
ICF type 1 arises from biallelic variants in DNMT3B, a DNA methyltransferase, while other types result from ZBTB24, CDCA7 or HELLS variants affecting the same methylation pathway
The underlying defect is hypomethylation of satellite DNA, linking an epigenetic abnormality to the immune and chromosomal phenotype
Immunoglobulin replacement and infection prophylaxis are the mainstays, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been used in severe immunodeficiency
reference.pathophysiology: ICF syndrome is an inherited disorder of DNA methylation. In the commonest form, biallelic loss-of-function variants in the DNA methyltransferase DNMT3B, or in the related factors ZBTB24, CDCA7 or HELLS, impair methylation of satellite repeat DNA in pericentromeric heterochromatin. The resulting hypomethylation destabilises these regions, producing the characteristic centromeric chromosomal rearrangements, and disturbs the regulated gene-expression programmes needed for normal lymphocyte development and terminal B-cell differentiation. Consequently, although B cells may be present, they fail to mature into effective antibody-secreting cells, giving hypogammaglobulinaemia and a predominantly humoral immunodeficiency, with variable T-cell involvement and the associated developmental and facial features.
additionalDifferentials: Other chromosomal instability syndromes (e.g. Nijmegen breakage syndrome, Bloom syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype or cytogenetic analysis demonstrating pericentromeric instability of chromosomes 1, 9 and 16
Serum immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets to assess B and T cell numbers
Assays of satellite DNA methylation where available
Sequencing of DNMT3B and, if negative, ZBTB24, CDCA7 and HELLS
redFlags: Overwhelming or recurrent severe infection reflecting profound antibody deficiency
Signs of opportunistic infection suggesting significant T-cell involvement
Failure to thrive with chronic gastrointestinal infection
Features suggesting evolving malignancy in a chromosomal instability disorder
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of the antibody deficiency and any T-cell involvement; recurrent infection can be life-limiting, but immunoglobulin replacement improves outcome and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered where cellular immunity is severely affected.
pitfalls: Diagnosing common variable immunodeficiency without recognising the syndromic and cytogenetic clues
Not requesting cytogenetics, thereby missing the diagnostic centromeric instability
Assuming the presence of B cells excludes a significant antibody deficiency
Attributing the facial and developmental features to an unrelated syndrome
Overlooking the epigenetic basis and the possible need for transplantation in severe cases
references: Stiehm's Immunologic Disorders in Infants and Children
IUIS Expert Committee classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Immunoglobulin replacement therapy as the mainstay for the humoral immunodeficiency and hypogammaglobulinaemia
Prompt antimicrobial treatment of sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections, with antibiotic prophylaxis where infections are recurrent
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation considered where cellular immunity is severely impaired
Avoidance of live vaccines and attention to infection-control measures given the immunodeficiency
Developmental, audiological and nutritional support with multidisciplinary paediatric and immunology input
Surveillance of immunoglobulin levels, lymphocyte subsets and infection frequency to guide therapy
Genetic counselling and family testing, reflecting autosomal recessive inheritance
